lessons.description: Practice the five short vowel sounds: a, e, i, o, u.

explanation.recap: Practice saying the five short vowel sounds in the words given, then try to use them in your own simple sentences.
explanation.overview: In this lesson you will learn the five short vowel sounds a, e, i, o, u. They appear in many everyday words, so knowing them helps you read and speak clearly. After the lesson you will be able to say and recognise these sounds in simple words.

sections.body:
- Short vowels are the quick sounds in words like cat or bed.
- They are different from the long sounds you hear in name or see.
- English has five short vowel sounds: a, e, i, o, u.
sections.heading: What are short vowels

sections.body:
- **a**: open your mouth a little, tongue low, say /æ/ as in cat.
- **e**: smile slightly, tongue mid, say /e/ as in bed.
- **i**: keep mouth relaxed, tongue high, say /ɪ/ as in sit.
- **o**: round lips a little, tongue low, say /ɒ/ as in hot.
- **u**: lips relaxed, tongue low, say /ʌ/ as in cup.
sections.heading: How to make each sound

sections.body:
- Read each word slowly and repeat the vowel sound.
- Use the words in short sentences to hear the sound in context.
- Listen to a friend say the words and try to copy exactly.
sections.heading: Practice with simple words

examples.note: short a in cat and mat
examples.text: The cat is on the mat.
I have a cup of tea.

keyPoints: There are only five short vowel sounds: a, e, i, o, u.
Short a sounds like the a in cat, not like the a in name.
Short e sounds like the e in bed, not like the e in see.
Short i sounds like the i in sit, not like the i in kite.
Short o sounds like the o in hot, not like the o in home.
Short u sounds like the u in cup, not like the u in music.

commonMistakes.why: Arabic speakers often stretch the vowel
commonMistakes.wrong: Saying a long vowel like /eɪ/ in cat

commonMistakes.why: Short vowels are quick
commonMistakes.right: Keep the sound brief and stop after one beat
commonMistakes.wrong: Adding an extra vowel after the short sound, e.g., ‘caaat’

commonMistakes.why: The short i is lower and shorter
commonMistakes.right: Use the short /ɪ/ as in sit
commonMistakes.wrong: Pronouncing i as /iː/ like in machine

commonMistakes.why: Over‑rounding changes the sound to a long o
commonMistakes.right: Make a small round shape, not a big one
commonMistakes.wrong: Rounding lips too much for short o

lessons.system_prompt: You are teaching short vowel sounds (a as in cat, e as in bed, i as in sit, o as in hot, u as in cup) to a true beginner. Demonstrate each sound, give one simple example word per vowel, and have the student practice saying the sound and the word. Keep instructions extremely short and concrete.

lessons.description: Listen to and practice tricky consonant sounds like p/b, f/v, and blends like "bl", "st".

explanation.recap: Listen to the audio, repeat each word, and then try the practice sentences out loud.
explanation.overview: In this lesson you will hear the small differences between the sounds p and b, f and v, and learn how to say simple blends like bl and st. Knowing these sounds helps you understand and be understood in everyday English. After the lesson you can tell the difference and say the words correctly.

sections.body:
- p is a soft puff of air, no voice.
- b uses the voice, like a short buzz.
- Listen for the breath on p and the buzz on b.
sections.heading: p and b sounds

examples.note: shows the puff (p) and buzz (b) at the start

sections.body:
- f is made without voice, just air.
- v adds voice, a small vibration.
- Feel the throat: no buzz for f, buzz for v.
sections.heading: f and v sounds

examples.note: first sound f is quiet, v is voiced
shows the difference in the middle

sections.body:
- A blend means two consonants are spoken together quickly.
- bl sounds like “b” then “l” in one smooth motion.
- st sounds like “s” then “t” without a vowel between.
- Practice saying the pair as one piece.
sections.heading: Common blends: bl and st

examples.note: bl blend followed by a vowel
st blend followed by a vowel

sections.body:
- Use the sounds you learned in short sentences.
- Say each sentence slowly, feeling the breath or buzz.
- Try to copy the rhythm of a native speaker.
sections.heading: Simple practice sentences

examples.note: contains b, bl, and b sounds
contains p, f, and st sounds

examples.text: Van and Van are very fast.

keyPoints: p is a puff of air, b adds voice
f is quiet, v vibrates the throat
bl and st are spoken together, no extra vowel
Listen for breath (p, f) or buzz (b, v)
Practice slowly, then speed up

v is missing because it is not in Arabic
Adding a vowel between blend letters breaks the blend
A pause adds an extra sound that should not be there

explanation.recap: Practice saying, listening to, and writing the numbers eleven to twenty until they feel natural.
explanation.overview: In this lesson you will learn the English words for the numbers eleven to twenty. Knowing these numbers lets you talk about age, money, time and many daily situations. After the lesson you will be able to say, recognize and write numbers 11‑20 correctly.

sections.body:

sections.heading: Words for 11‑20

sections.body:
- The sound **th** in thirteen is soft, like the **th** in *think*. Only thirteen has this sound; eleven and fourteen to nineteen do not.
- Stress: *eleven* is stressed on the second syllable (e-LEV-en), and *twelve* has only one syllable. Thirteen to nineteen are stressed on -teen when you say them alone (thir-TEEN). Before a noun the stress often moves to the first syllable (THIR-teen PEO-ple).
- Say the whole word, not the digit plus "ten" (for example, say *eleven* not *one ten*).
sections.heading: How to say them

examples.note: stress on the second syllable: e-LEV-en
soft th sound; stress on -teen: thir-TEEN
stress on -teen when said alone: seven-TEEN

sections.body:
- Put the number word before the noun.
- Use the plural form of the noun when the number is more than one.
- You can also use the number to tell age or time.
sections.heading: Using numbers in sentences

examples.text: My brother is fifteen years old.
The class starts at eleven o'clock.

sections.body:
- Write the number as a digit when you can.
- The digit matches the spoken word.
- Practice matching the word to the digit.
sections.heading: Writing the digits

keyPoints: eleven to twenty are single words, not "ten‑one" etc.
the "th" sound in thirteen is soft, like in think
eleven is stressed on the second syllable (e-LEV-en); thirteen to nineteen are stressed on -teen when said alone (thir-TEEN), and the stress may move to the first syllable before a noun
place the number word before the noun
the digit 13 matches the word thirteen

The ordinal form (fifteenth) is different from the cardinal (fifteen)

lessons.description: Learn the most common greetings and farewells.

explanation.recap: Practice greeting people, saying goodbye, and introducing yourself with your name in short conversations.
explanation.overview: In this lesson you will learn the most common ways to say hello and goodbye. You will also learn how to greet people at different times of day and how to introduce yourself by name. After the lesson you can greet strangers and say farewell in simple English.

sections.body:
- Use short words to start a conversation.
- "Hello" works any time of day.
- "Hi" is informal and friendly.
- "Hey" is very casual with friends.
sections.heading: Simple greetings

sections.body:
- Match the greeting to the time.
- "Good morning" is used until about 12 pm.
- "Good afternoon" is from 12 pm to about 6 pm.
- "Good evening" is after 6 pm.
- You can still say "Hello" at any time.
sections.heading: Time‑of‑day greetings

sections.body:
- Use short words to end a conversation.
- "Goodbye" is polite and works any time.
- "Bye" is informal and common.
- You can add "see you later" for a friendly tone.
sections.heading: Saying goodbye

sections.body:
- State your name after a greeting.
- Use "I am" or "My name is".
- Keep it short and clear.
- You can add a friendly word like "nice to meet you".
- Example: "Hello, I am Ali."
sections.heading: Introducing yourself

examples.text: Good morning, I am Omar. Nice to meet you.

keyPoints: Hello and Hi are everyday greetings
Good morning/afternoon/evening match the time of day
Goodbye is polite; Bye is informal
Use I am or My name is to give your name
Add Nice to meet you after your name for politeness

commonMistakes.why: Use "Good evening" for night time
Avoid extra words that sound unnatural
The correct phrase is "My name is"
Do not mix time greetings with the wrong name

lessons.system_prompt: Teach "hello", "hi", "good morning/afternoon/evening", "goodbye", and "bye" to a true beginner. Model each phrase and have the student practice a short greeting exchange with you.

lessons.description: Listen to a short dialogue between two people meeting for the first time.

explanation.recap: Listen to the dialogue again, repeat each sentence, and try to say the same greetings, name questions, and goodbyes yourself.
explanation.overview: In this lesson you will hear a short conversation where two people meet for the first time. You will learn the most common greetings, how to ask and give your name, and how to say goodbye. After listening you will be able to follow a simple introduction dialogue.

sections.body:
- Hello
- Hi
- Good morning
- Good afternoon
sections.heading: Greetings

examples.note: Shows a common greeting followed by a name
Another simple greeting with a name

sections.body:
- What is your name?
- My name is ...
- I am ...
sections.heading: Asking and Giving Your Name

examples.note: Another way to give your name

sections.body:
- Nice to meet you
- Goodbye
- See you later
sections.heading: Goodbyes

examples.note: Simple way to end the conversation

sections.body:
- Listen for the words Hello, Hi, What is your name?, My name is, Goodbye.
- Pay attention to the speaker’s tone; friendly tone means a greeting.
- Count the number of short sentences; most introductions have three parts: greeting, name exchange, goodbye.
sections.heading: Listening Tips

examples.note: Typical structure of a short introduction
examples.text: Hello, my name is Anna. What is your name? My name is Ahmed. Nice to meet you. Goodbye!

keyPoints: Use Hello or Hi to start a conversation
Ask What is your name? to learn the other person’s name
Answer with My name is … or I am …
Finish with Nice to meet you or Goodbye
Listen for the three parts: greeting, name exchange, goodbye

commonMistakes.why: Arabic often drops the question word, but English needs the whole question
The pronoun My is needed to sound natural
Bye bye is informal and may sound childish for first meetings
Use only one greeting at a time

lessons.system_prompt: Present a short listening dialogue of two people greeting each other and introducing themselves, then check the student's comprehension by asking who said what.

lessons.description: Listen and respond to common classroom commands.

explanation.recap: Listen to each command, pause, and practice saying the short response. Keep practicing until the answers feel natural.
explanation.overview: In this lesson you will hear common classroom commands and learn how to answer them. Knowing these phrases helps you follow instructions in any class. After the lesson you will understand the commands and be able to respond correctly.

sections.body:
- Listen carefully to the teacher.
- Recognize the key word.
- Remember the short answer you need.
sections.heading: Common classroom commands

examples.note: Command to turn to a page
Command to show you want to speak
examples.text: Raise your hand if you have a question.

sections.body:
- Use a short polite answer.
- Keep your response simple.
- Show that you have understood.
sections.heading: How to respond

examples.text: Sure, I am opening it now.
Yes, I have raised my hand.
Sorry, I will close it now.

sections.body:
- Listen to the audio once.
- Pause and repeat the command.
- Say the correct response out loud.
- Check if your answer matches the model.
sections.heading: Practice listening and answering

examples.text: Listen: "Write your name on the paper."

keyPoints: Listen for the main verb in the command
Answer with a short polite phrase
Use "I will" for actions you will do now
Use "I have" for actions you already did

commonMistakes.why: Add a polite answer, not just repeat the command
Use a full sentence with a verb
commonMistakes.right: Sure, I am opening it now.

commonMistakes.why: Answer positively, not with a question
commonMistakes.right: Yes, I have raised my hand.

commonMistakes.why: Include a polite word and correct verb form
commonMistakes.right: Sorry, I will close it now.

lessons.system_prompt: Teach common classroom commands: "Listen", "Repeat", "Write", "Open your book", "Look at the screen". Play each command and ask the student to say what it means or act it out in words.

lessons.description: Learn basic family member vocabulary: mother, father, sister, brother.

explanation.recap: Practice naming each family member with 'my' and answering simple questions about them.
explanation.overview: In this lesson you will learn the four most common family words: mother, father, sister and brother. Knowing these words lets you talk about the people who live with you. After the lesson you will be able to name each family member correctly in short sentences.

sections.body:
- mother: your female parent
- father: your male parent
- sister: a female sibling
- brother: a male sibling
sections.heading: Family words list

examples.note: Shows how to point to a female parent
Shows father as subject of a sentence

sections.body:
- My mother works.
- My father reads.
- My sister sings.
- My brother plays.
sections.heading: Simple sentences with family words

sections.body:
- I have a mother and a father.
- I have one sister.
- I have two brothers.
- My family is small.
sections.heading: Talking about your own family

examples.text: I have a mother and a father.

examples.note: Uses family word in a description

sections.body:
- Who is this? – She is my sister.
- Who is he? – He is my brother.
- Who is your mother? – She is my mother.
- Who is your father? – He is my father.
sections.heading: Answering simple questions

examples.text: Who is this? She is my sister.
Who is he? He is my brother.
Who is your mother? She is my mother.
Who is your father? He is my father.

keyPoints: Family words are nouns that name people you are related to
Use 'my' before the word to show that the person is yours
The verb 'to be' (am/is/are) is often used with family words
When you point to someone, you can say 'This is my …'
Plural forms (mothers, fathers) are not needed for this beginner lesson

commonMistakes.why: You need a word like 'my' to show ownership
Use 'my' before the family word, not 'I am'
Add the article 'a' when you talk about one family member
Use the possessive form 'your' when asking about someone’s family

ar_existing.title: عبارات البقاء اليومية
ar_existing.description: تعلّم العبارات الأساسية: please, thank you, sorry, excuse me, yes, no.

lessons.description: Learn essential phrases: please, thank you, sorry, excuse me, yes, no.

explanation.recap: Practice these six phrases in real conversations until they feel natural.
explanation.overview: In this lesson you will learn short polite words that help you survive everyday situations. You will be able to ask for help, thank people, apologize, and answer simple questions in English.

sections.body:
- Use **please** when you want something.
- Say **thank you** after someone helps you.
- Both words make you sound friendly.
sections.heading: Polite requests

examples.text: Can you pass the salt, please?

sections.body:
- Say **sorry** when you make a mistake.
- Use **excuse me** to get someone's attention or to pass by.
- Both are useful in crowded places.
sections.heading: Apologizing and getting attention

examples.text: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

sections.body:
- **Yes** and **no** answer questions directly.
- Say **I don’t understand** when you need more explanation.
- Keep the sentences short and clear.
sections.heading: Simple answers and clarification

keyPoints: Please adds politeness to requests
Thank you shows appreciation
Sorry apologizes for a mistake
Excuse me gets attention or lets you pass
Yes and no give clear answers
I don’t understand asks for help

commonMistakes.why: Swap order; thank you comes first
Use one at a time for clarity
Do not combine opposite answers

lessons.system_prompt: Teach essential survival phrases (please, thank you, sorry, excuse me, yes, no, I don't understand) to a true beginner with simple usage examples.
